home.title: Really learn C#. Then make your own game.
home.lead: A short bit of theory, then a task right away. Code runs right in the browser, and tests honestly tell you what works.

errors.network: No connection to the server. Check your internet.

runner.loading: Loading the C# compiler. The first time takes a few seconds.
runner.timeout: The program ran too long, so we stopped it. Maybe it has an endless loop — a loop whose condition never becomes false.
runner.crashed: The compiler stopped unexpectedly. Try running again.
runner.outputLimit: The program printed too much text, so we stopped it. Maybe printing is inside an endless loop.

compiler.unknown: The compiler found an error. Its explanation is below.
compiler.unknownWarning: The compiler warns you: the program will run, but check this place. Its explanation is below.
compiler.CS1002: A semicolon «;» is missing. In C# every command ends with «;» — that is how the computer knows where it ends.
compiler.CS0103: The name «{arg0}» was not found. Check that it is declared and spelled without typos. C# tells capital and small letters apart: «hp» and «HP» are different names.
compiler.CS0246: The type «{arg0}» was not found. A type is a kind of data: int is a whole number, string is text. Check the spelling.
compiler.CS0029: A value of type {arg0} can't go into a variable of type {arg1}. For example, text in quotes is a string, not a number.
compiler.CS0266: A value of type {arg0} can't just go into {arg1}: some data may be lost — for example, the fractional part of a number.
compiler.CS0165: The variable «{arg0}» is used, but nothing has been put into it yet. Assign a value before reading a variable.
compiler.CS0128: The name «{arg0}» is already taken — a variable or a method already has it. Choose another name. If you want to change the value of a variable that already exists, remove the type before the name: «hp = 85;» instead of «int hp = 85;».
compiler.CS1010: The text is not closed: a quote «"» is missing at the end of the line.
compiler.CS1513: A closing curly brace «{'}'}» is missing. Every «{'{'}» needs its pair.
compiler.CS1026: A closing parenthesis «)» is missing. Every «(» needs its pair.
compiler.CS0117: {arg0} has no «{arg1}». Check the spelling: C# tells capital and small letters apart.
compiler.CS1061: A value of type {arg0} has no «{arg1}». Check the spelling: C# tells capital and small letters apart.
compiler.CS0019: The operation «{arg0}» can't be done with values of types {arg1} and {arg2}. For example, you can't subtract a number from text.
compiler.CS1501: The method «{arg0}» doesn't take this many arguments ({arg1}). Arguments are the values in parentheses when you call a method.
compiler.CS0161: The method {arg0} must return a value, but there is a case where it ends without return.
compiler.CS0201: This line does nothing. A command can be, for example, an assignment (hp = 10) or a method call (Console.WriteLine(hp)).
compiler.CS1525: «{arg0}» can't be here: a value or an expression is needed in this place.
compiler.CS0219: A value was put into the variable «{arg0}», but it is never used after that.
compiler.CS0168: The variable «{arg0}» is declared but never used.
compiler.CS8773: This can't be written in C# 9: it appeared in C# {arg1}. We learn C# 9 — the version Unity understands. Try writing it another way.
compiler.CS8803: Program commands must come before class declarations: commands first, classes at the end of the file.
compiler.CS1001: A name is expected here — for example, a variable name. If you wrote a decimal number, separate the fraction with a dot: 0.3, not 0,3.
compiler.CS5001: The program has no commands to run. Add at least one, for example printing with Console.WriteLine.
compiler.CS7036: An argument for the parameter «{arg0}» of the method {arg1} is missing. When calling a method, pass a value for every parameter — in order, separated by commas.
compiler.CS1503: Argument #{arg0}: a value of type {arg1} doesn't fit a parameter of type {arg2}. Compare the order and types of the arguments with the method declaration.
compiler.CS8421: A method marked static can't see «{arg0}» from the main code. If it is a variable, pass its value through a parameter and give the new value back with return. If it is a method, mark it static too.
compiler.CS0127: The method {arg0} is declared with void — it returns nothing, so return must not be followed by a value. Write just «return;» or replace void with the type of the answer.
compiler.CS0126: The method must return a value of type {arg0}, but return has no value. Write the method's answer after return, for example «return hp;».
compiler.CS0106: The word «{arg0}» can't be written here — remove it. In the main code, methods and variables are written without public and private.
compiler.CS0428: «{arg0}» is the name of a method, not its answer. To call the method, add parentheses: {arg0}().
compiler.CS0136: The name «{arg0}» is already taken in an outer block — for example, by a variable declared above, before the loop. A block is code in curly braces. Give this variable another name.
compiler.CS8321: The method «{arg0}» is declared but never called. It is not an error, but its commands won't run without a call.
compiler.CS1003: A writing mistake: the symbol «{arg0}» should be here. Check whether it is missing — for example, a comma between values: {'{'} 1, 2, 3 {'}'}.
compiler.CS0162: The program never gets to this place, so the commands here won't run. This happens when a command comes after break, continue or return: they leave the loop or the method at once. Move the command higher or remove it.
compiler.CS0642: There is a semicolon «;» right after if (…), for (…) or while (…). It ends the command: the condition or the loop stops here, and the block in curly braces below always runs — once and without a check. And while (…); can loop forever: the loop has no body, so the condition never changes. Remove the «;» after the parentheses.
compiler.CS0020: Division by zero: the number you divide by is 0. You can't divide by zero — use another number.
compiler.CS0023: The operation «{arg0}» can't be applied to a value of type {arg1}. For example, «!» («not») works only with true and false (type bool): !alive is fine, but !hp is not. Compare a number first: hp <= 0.
compiler.CS0841: The variable «{arg0}» is used before it is declared. The program runs from top to bottom — move the line that declares «{arg0}» above this one.
compiler.CS1012: Single quotes hold exactly one character: 'a' is a char. Text of several characters goes in double quotes: "abc" is a string.
compiler.CS0664: A number with a dot (for example, 2.5) is a double in C#. To put it into {arg1}, add the letter {arg0} at the end: for float — 2.5f, for decimal — 2.5m.
compiler.CS0200: «{arg0}» can only be read, not changed. For example, the length of an array (Length) is set once, when it is created: new int[4]. Need a different number of elements — create a new array.
compiler.CS1955: «{arg0}» is not a method, so it has no parentheses after it. For example, the length of a text is name.Length, without (). Parentheses are needed only to call a method: name.ToUpper().
compiler.CS1656: You can't put a value into «{arg0}»: it is not a variable. For example, a method name is not a place for a value: a method is called with parentheses.
compiler.CS1526: After new and the type you need brackets: round ones — new Random(), square ones with a size — new int[3], or curly ones with values — new int[] {'{'} 1, 2 {'}'}.
compiler.CS0030: A value of type {arg0} can't be turned into {arg1}. For example, (int) doesn't turn text into a number: (int)"5" won't work.
compiler.CS0847: The array length in square brackets doesn't match the number of values in curly braces: there should be {arg0} values. Fix the number in [ ] or remove it — C# will count by itself: new int[] {'{'} 1, 2, 3 {'}'}.
compiler.CS1579: A value of type {arg0} can't be looped over with foreach: you can only loop over a set of elements — an array, a list or a text. Check that a set, not a single value, comes after in.
compiler.CS0665: The condition has a single «=» — it puts a value into the variable instead of comparing. To compare, write two signs: ==.
compiler.CS1660: There is «=>» here — that is how C# writes a lambda (a short form of a method), but a value of type {arg1} is needed. If you compare «greater than or equal», write >=: hp >= 5.
compiler.CS0122: «{arg0}» can be accessed only inside its class — make it public if you need it outside.
compiler.CS0120: «{arg0}» is used through an object, not through the class name. First create an object — for example, Hero hero = new Hero(); — and use it: hero.hp. If the value is shared by all objects, mark it with the word static.
compiler.CS0104: The name «{arg0}» exists in two namespaces (sets of types you connect with using): {arg1} and {arg2}. C# doesn't know which one to take. Write the full name, for example {arg2}, or rename your class.
compiler.CS8801: «{arg0}» from the main code can't be seen inside a class: variables and methods of the main code are available only there. Pass the value into the class through a constructor or method parameter, or make «{arg0}» a part of the class itself.
compiler.CS0542: A field or a method can't have the same name as its class («{arg0}»). Give it another name. If it is a constructor, write it without a return type: public {arg0}(), without void.
compiler.CS0272: The set of «{arg0}» is private: the value can be changed only inside the class, and outside it can only be read. Change the value through a method of the class.
compiler.CS1729: The class {arg0} has no constructor that takes this many arguments ({arg1}). Compare them with the constructor parameters. When a class has its own constructor, the empty one — new {arg0}() — no longer appears by itself: add it if you need it.
compiler.CS0649: Nothing is ever put into the field «{arg0}», so it will always be {arg1} — the default value. Assign it, for example, in the constructor.
compiler.CS1717: A variable is assigned to itself — nothing changes. If a constructor parameter has the same name as a field, write this.hp = hp: this.hp is the object's field, and hp is the parameter.
compiler.CS0176: «{arg0}» is marked static — it belongs to the class, not to an object. Remove static from a method or field of an object, and use a static member through the class name: {arg0}.

compilerCases.voidInInterpolation: Inside the curly braces $"…{'{'} {'}'}" there is a call of a void method. Such a method returns nothing — there is nothing to put into the text. If the method should answer, replace void with the type of the answer and return a value with return.
compilerCases.interpolationValue: Inside the curly braces $"…{'{'} {'}'}" there is something that can't be put into text. You can put values there: variables, numbers and calls of methods that return an answer.
compilerCases.voidValue: The method returns nothing (void), so its result can't be put into a variable or passed on. If the method should answer, replace void with the type of the answer and return a value with return.
compilerCases.methodGroup: There is a method name without parentheses here — that is not a call yet. To call the method and get its answer, add parentheses, for example Damage().
compilerCases.assignInCondition: Here is a value of type {arg0}, but true or false is needed. If you compare, write two signs ==; a single = puts a value into a variable.
compilerCases.countOrLength: A list's number of elements is Count, an array's is Length.
compilerCases.missingSeparator: A sign is missing: most likely «;» at the end of a command on this line or above, or «,» between values.
compilerCases.foreachVariable: You can't assign a new value to «{arg0}»: it is a foreach loop variable, it only shows the elements one by one. To change an array element, use a for loop and an index — the element's number: items[i] = 5.
compilerCases.stringChar: A character in a string can't be changed: a string in C# doesn't change after it is created. Build a new string from the parts you need and put it into the variable.

runtime.unknown: The program stopped with the error {type}.
runtime.DivideByZeroException: Division by zero. A whole number can't be divided by zero — check the divisor.
runtime.IndexOutOfRangeException: The array has no element with this number. Numbers (indexes) start at 0: in an array of 3 elements the last one is 2.
runtime.ArgumentOutOfRangeException: A number is out of the allowed range. For example, a list element number is bigger than the number of elements.
runtime.NullReferenceException: Access to an empty value (null): the variable doesn't point to anything.
runtime.FormatException: The text is not written the way it should be. For example, the text «ten» can't be turned into a number — it needs «10».
runtime.OverflowException: The number is too big or too small for this type.
runtime.InvalidCastException: The value can't be turned into this type.
runtime.KeyNotFoundException: The dictionary has no such key.
runtime.InvalidOperationException: This action can't be done right now. For example, you can't add or remove list elements while a foreach loop goes through the list, and you can't take the first element of an empty list.

task.compileErrors: The program doesn't compile. Fix the errors — they are underlined in the code:

checks.output: The program prints what is needed
checks.outputWith: The program prints what is needed when {values}
checks.variableTyped: There is a variable {name} of type {type}
checks.access: The value {name} of a {type} object is used

constructs.continue: continue (jumping to the next loop step)
constructs.privateSet: private set (can be changed only inside the class)
constructs.this: this (a field of its own object)

setError.notFound: This check runs the program with another value of {variable}, but there is no variable {variable} in the main code. Declare it with a value at the start of the program, outside loops and methods, as in the starting code, and don't rename it.
setError.noValue: The variable {variable} is declared without a starting value. Give it a value right in the declaration, as in the starting code: type {variable} = value;
setError.wrongType: The variable {variable} has the type {type}, but the check puts a value of another type into it. Keep the type as in the starting code.
setError.notCompiled: The program was checked with another value of {variable}, but the code doesn't compile with it. Check that {variable} is used as an ordinary variable that doesn't rely on one particular value.
